label: Youth programmes in the US: shared figures

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per standard deviation of a one-year childhood gain (share of earnings)

source.title: Chetty, Friedman and Rockoff, 'Measuring the Impacts of Teachers II: Teacher Value-Added and Student Outcomes in Adulthood', American Economic Review 2014 (NBER Working Paper 19424, revision 2)
source.quote: On average, a one standard deviation improvement in teacher VA in a single grade raises earnings by 1.3% at age 28.

rows.explainer: A teacher one standard deviation better in value-added raises a year's test scores by about 0.12 SD in maths and 0.08 SD in English (the same authors' summary, 'Great Teaching: Measuring Its Effects on Students' Future Earnings', Education Next 2012, https://www.educationnext.org/great-teaching/) and earnings at 28 by 1.3%: 1.3% ÷ 0.10 SD (the average of maths and English) = about 13% per SD of a one-year test gain, measured in adulthood, so the fade-out of test scores is already in it (in Project STAR too, classroom-quality effects fade on tests and re-emerge in earnings: Chetty and others, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2011). 10%, from 5% to 13%: below CFR's 13% because much of youth programmes' gain is in social-emotional or self-reported outcomes, which predict earnings less than test gains; the models that read this count that doubt here only. Read by every charityevals model of US children's and youth programmes (United Way, Boys & Girls Clubs of America).
